blocks.text: Mass spectrometry can find the relative abundance of isotopes experimentally. The relative abundance is the proportion of a particular isotope in the natural mixture of isotopes; for example, chlorine is 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37. The heights of the peaks in a mass spectrum show the proportion of each isotope: for boron, B-10 has a relative abundance of 19.9% and B-11 of 80.1%.

blocks.alt: Mass spectrum of boron: % abundance against m/e, with a short yellow bar at m/e 10 labelled 19.9 and a tall green bar at m/e 11 labelled 80.1.
blocks.caption: Mass spectrum of boron (original drawing after the spectrum printed in 29.6.1).

blocks.title: Relative atomic mass
blocks.text: The relative atomic mass, Ar, of an element is the average mass of its isotopes: Ar = sum of (isotopic mass x percentage abundance) / 100. The abundances are given or read from the mass spectrum.
